title: Fall
lede: Bridget Riley’s 1963 painting of a single wave line repeated across the surface, with waves that tighten toward the bottom until the field seems to ripple.
summary: Hundreds of thin black and white vertical waves whose curves compress toward the base. Bridget Riley, Tate, 1963.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Tate’s image of T00616 (1196 × 1200 px) from media.tate.org.uk in a scratchpad. The artwork page renders most of its text with JavaScript; the medium was read from the page metadata. No image is stored.

styles.note: A canonical black and white op painting: one curved stripe repeated edge to edge, with a period that changes by steps to make the surface seem to move.

context: Tate lists *Fall*, 1963, as polyvinyl acetate paint on hardboard, collection number T00616, on display at Tate Britain in the Bridget Riley room. [Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/riley-fall-t00616).

Riley’s *Current* (1964), a painting of the same kind, was reproduced on the cover of [The Responsive Eye](ref:the-responsive-eye-catalogue-1965) catalogue in 1965. [David Zwirner](https://www.davidzwirner.com/news/2019/bridget-riley-s-paintings-continue-to-mesmerize-six-decades-on).
observed: Thin vertical black and white stripes of almost equal width fill the square surface to all four edges.
Every stripe follows the same wavy path. In the upper part the waves are long and gentle; toward the bottom they become shorter and sharper.
In the lowest band the waves are so tight that the stripes seem to vibrate and form moiré-like ridges.
The black is slightly warm and the white slightly off-white in the photograph. There is no other colour and no texture beyond the paint.
interpretation: *Fall* is the reference case for the style’s “progression and distortion” grammar: nothing changes except the period of one repeated curve.
It shows why op patterns need a fixed size on screen: the effect depends on the width of each stripe relative to the eye.
borrow: Repeat one wave path hundreds of times with a small horizontal offset, and shorten its period toward one edge.
Fill the whole panel edge to edge so that the field has no frame inside it.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is by a living artist, and Tate’s image is not openly licensed.
